abstract: Solid-state refrigerators using Normal-metal/Insulator/Superconductor (NIS) junctions have previously demonstrated excellent electron cooling but limited ability to cool phonons. The energy gap of the superconductor is used as an energy filter to allow higher than average energy electrons to preferentially tunnel from the normal-metal through the insulator into the superconductor where they travel as quasi-particles. Typically, the heat is moved and work is done to deposit hot quasi-particles into a normal-metal quasi-particle trap for rejection to the next refrigeration stage. Realizing that (1) the quasi-particles flow diffusively, driven by a concentration gradient in the electric field-free superconductor, and (2) that the undesirable backwards leaking of heat from the hot-side trap can be reduced by engineering the geometry and materials at the superconductor-to-trap interface, enhanced cooling can be achieved. Fabrication of the refrigerator was accomplished using a tungsten and titanium-tungsten alloy as the cold-side normal-metal, aluminum oxide as the insulator, aluminum as the superconductor, and gold as the trap, with the cold-side NIS portion being attached to the hot-side gold trap by bump bonding. The refrigerator consisted of 1121 junction pairs, each pair being an SINIS unit, all electrically connected in series. Using this we have measured the effective phonon temperature of a 3.9 mm x 3.9 mm x 0.65 mm silicon chip driven down to 70 mK from a bath temperature of 120 mK, and down to 174 mK from a 271 mK rejection temperature (a cooling of -97 mK). This is the first demonstration of the sub 1 K cooling of an entire silicon chip using NIS junctions.
summary: This paper reports on the design and experimental realization of a solid-state refrigerator that cools silicon chips to sub-Kelvin temperatures using arrays of NIS superconducting junctions. The methodology involves modeling quasi-particle diffusion and meticulously engineering the interfaces to minimize parasitic heat leakage. The success demonstrates a significant advance in solid-state cryocooling technology.
main_problem: To develop a scalable, solid-state refrigerator capable of cooling silicon chips to temperatures below 1 K by efficiently managing heat transfer and minimizing parasitic heat leakage.
main_result: The authors demonstrated cooling of a silicon chip down to 70 mK and achieved a cooling of -97 mK, marking the first demonstration of sub-1 K cooling of an entire silicon chip using NIS junctions.
method: The work combines experimental fabrication of complex superconducting junctions with advanced 3D numerical simulations to model quasi-particle diffusion and interfacial heat flow.
model_or_system: The system is a chip-scale refrigerator built from Normal-metal/Insulator/Superconductor (NIS) junctions, configured as SINIS units, which operate by filtering electrons via the superconducting energy gap. Heat transport is modeled using diffusive quasi-particle flow, incorporating both Acoustic Mismatch Models (AMM) and specific interfacial heat flow equations.
key_observables: Effective phonon temperature of the silicon chip, Coefficient of Performance (COP), and 2nd Law Efficiency.
important_parameters: Operating temperatures down to 70 mK, junction resistance ($	ext{621 } \Omega\cdot\mu	ext{m}^2$), and the superconducting energy gap ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve modeling quasi-particle flow as diffusive and engineering the geometry to limit heat leakage, though some models ignore quasiparticle branching mixing effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lithography masks and cross-sections of the cooler, schematics of the SINIS unit, and comparative plots showing simulated vs. experimental phonon temperature profiles validating the heat leakage model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical limitations of existing coolers to detailing the NIS junction physics, developing sophisticated models for heat leakage, and culminating in the measurement and validation of sub-Kelvin cooling performance metrics.
why_interesting: The detailed modeling of non-equilibrium heat transport, involving energy filtering via superconducting gaps and diffusive quasi-particle dynamics, touches upon non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and energy relaxation processes relevant to quantum thermodynamics.
